name: Ear training

lead: Ear training teaches you to recognise pitches, intervals, melodies and rhythms by ear. In voice discussions it is borrowed to build awareness of vocal pitch and a more intentional tone.

It is a core part of formal music education, using solfege, interval and chord recognition, rhythm exercises and apps. Its use for voice appearance is anecdotal, and no studies have tested it for attractiveness outcomes.

paras: People do short listening and identification exercises with apps or a teacher, then try to match and control pitch with their own voice.

web.title: Reestablishing speech understanding through musical ear training after cochlear implantation

angle.text: Learning to recognise pitches by ear gives better awareness and control of your own vocal pitch, for a more intentional voice tone. It is established for music skills and borrowed for voice.

lead: Ear training is the practice of learning to identify pitches, intervals, melodies, chords and rhythms by listening alone, a standard part of music education [1][2]. In looksmaxxing and voice-focused discussion it is borrowed as a way to hear one's own pitch and tone more precisely, so that a deeper, steadier or more expressive speaking voice can be practiced and matched to a target. Voice is part of how a person comes across, which is why it appears next to posture and grooming in presence-oriented self-improvement.

Methods include solfege, interval and chord recognition, rhythm and timbre exercises, transcription, partner drills and software or smartphone apps [1]. Wikipedia describes relative pitch (identifying notes against a reference) and perfect pitch (identifying notes with no reference) as the two broad abilities involved [1].

Ear training also appears in clinical voice work. A 2022 review of gender-affirming behavioural voice modification lists ear training, direct vocal modelling and mastery of voice techniques as important elements of voice training [3], and a small 1996 Thai report on mutational falsetto described therapy that combined perceptual evaluation, ear training practice and establishing a new pitch, after which most of its seven patients' voices improved within five sessions [4]. No study has tested ear training for attractiveness or appearance outcomes.
infobox: Solfege, interval and chord recognition, dictation, rhythm drills [1]
Apps and software such as EarMaster, Auralia, Meludia, GNU Solfege [1]
Free to low-cost apps; lessons optional

paras: Ear training is described as roughly the inverse of reading music: instead of turning notation into sound, the learner turns sound into labels or notation [1]. Skills include functional pitch recognition (hearing a note's role relative to a tonic), interval and chord identification, rhythm, timbre and transcription [1]. Grokipedia traces the formal teaching of these skills to nineteenth-century conservatories and describes relative ear as more readily trained than absolute pitch [2].

Because voice pitch is controlled by what the speaker hears, training to hear small pitch differences is used in voice coaching. The 2022 review argues that ear training is among the crucial but under-emphasised elements of gender-affirming voice training, alongside modelling and technique practice [3]. The 1996 mutational falsetto report used ear training practice as one component of therapy for abnormally high pitch [4].
Within appearance-focused communities the same idea is applied informally to work on speaking pitch and tone, as part of a broader set of voice and presence habits.

Laboratory work shows that musical training is associated with finer pitch-interval discrimination: a 2017 study found expert musicians had lower discrimination thresholds than non-musicians and amateurs [5]. A 2009 study examined musical ear training in cochlear implant users for speech and music perception [6]. Related training studies include a 2017 trial of a programme to judge auditory source width, which found smaller errors after training [7].

No studies found for appearance or attractiveness outcomes. Studies in related areas are described above: a small case series using ear training within voice therapy for mutational falsetto [4], a review of voice modification training [3], and trials of musical ear training in cochlear implant users [6].
